The deviation on reflection is **180° − 2i**.
**Step 1 — find the angle of reflection.** By the law of reflection,
r = i = **60°** ✓
**Step 2 — find the angle between the incident and reflected directions.** The incident
ray would have continued straight on; instead it leaves on the other side of the
normal, so the deviation is
δ = 180° − 2i
= 180° − 120°
= **60°** ✓
**Why the formula takes that form.** The incident and reflected rays each make angle i
with the normal, so the angle **between** them is 2i ✓ The deviation from the original
direction is the supplement, 180° − 2i.
**Checking the extremes.**
**normal incidence**, i = 0: δ = **180°** ✓ the ray comes straight back
**grazing incidence**, i = 90°: δ = **0°** ✓ the ray skims past undeviated
**i = 45°**: δ = **90°** - a right-angle turn, which is why 45° mirrors are used in
periscopes ✓
**A caution about "angle of incidence".** It is measured from the **normal**, not from
the surface ✓ Taking 60° from the surface would mean i = 30° and δ = 120° - which is
the fourth option, and the designed trap.
**What happens with two mirrors.** For two mirrors at angle θ, a ray reflected from
both is deviated by **360° − 2θ** ✓ For perpendicular mirrors that is 180° - the ray
returns exactly parallel to itself, whatever the angle of incidence. This is the
principle of the **corner reflector**, used in cycle reflectors and in the retro-
reflectors left on the Moon.
**Why the mirror's own orientation does not appear.** Only the angle between the ray
and the **normal** matters ✓ Rotating the mirror by α rotates the reflected ray by
**2α** - a fact exploited in the optical lever and in galvanometer mirrors.
**The reflection is specular.** The surface is smooth compared with the wavelength, so
a parallel beam stays parallel ✓ A rough surface scatters diffusely, and no single
deviation can be quoted.
**Reading the distractors.** **120°** ✗ is 2i, the angle **between** the two rays
rather than the deviation. **30°** ✗ and **90°** ✗ correspond to i = 75° and 45° ✓
∴ 60°.

Laser action requires a **metastable** upper level, from which stimulated transitions
go to a **lower** level.
**Step 1 — recall why a metastable state is needed.** An ordinary excited state decays
spontaneously in about **10⁻⁸ s** - far too quickly to accumulate atoms there ✓ A
**metastable** state lives for **10⁻³ s** or longer, long enough for atoms to pile up.
**Step 2 — see what that makes possible.** **Population inversion** ✓ more atoms in the
upper state than in the lower - the essential condition for amplification rather than
absorption.
**Step 3 — identify the transition.** Stimulated emission then takes an atom from the
**metastable state** down to a **lower state** ✓ which need not be the ground state.
**Why not simply "to the ground state".** In the common **four-level** laser the lower
laser level is an **excited** state, not the ground state ✓ That is a great advantage:
the lower level empties rapidly into the ground state, so inversion is easy to
maintain. The Nd:YAG and the helium-neon lasers both work this way.
**Why not "any higher state".** Ordinary excited states decay too fast ✓ Atoms never
accumulate there, so no inversion forms and no laser action occurs.
**What makes stimulated emission special.** The emitted photon is **identical** to the
one that triggered it - same frequency, phase, direction and polarisation ✓ That is why
laser light is coherent, monochromatic and tightly collimated, whereas spontaneous
emission is random in all four respects.
**The three processes Einstein identified in 1917.**
**absorption**: photon in, atom up ✓
**spontaneous emission**: atom down, random photon ✓
**stimulated emission**: photon in, **two** identical photons out ✓
A laser is an engine for making the third dominate.
**The three requirements for a laser.**
a **metastable** level ✓
a **pumping** mechanism to create the inversion ✓
an **optical cavity** - two mirrors - to make the light pass many times ✓
**The acronym.** **L**ight **A**mplification by **S**timulated **E**mission of
**R**adiation ✓
∴ metastable state to any lower state.

In **common emitter** the emitter is shared, so the input goes between **base and
emitter**.
**Step 1 — see what "common emitter" means.** The **emitter** terminal is common to the
input and output circuits ✓ It is the reference point for both.
**Step 2 — identify the input.** The signal is applied between the **base** and the
**emitter** - the remaining input terminal and the common one ✓
**Step 3 — identify the output.** Taken between the **collector** and the emitter ✓
**Why the base-emitter junction is the input.** It is **forward biased**, so a small
change in V_BE produces a large change in base current ✓ and the transistor's current
gain β then multiplies that into a much larger collector current.
**Why the CE configuration is the most used.** It gives both **current** gain and
**voltage** gain, hence the largest **power** gain of the three ✓
current gain **β ≈ 100**
voltage gain of **100 or more** with a suitable load
power gain of **10⁴** or better
**Its characteristic phase inversion.** A rising input gives a **falling** output ✓ The
output is 180° out of phase with the input - a signature of the CE amplifier, and the
reason two stages are often cascaded to restore the phase.
**The input resistance.** A few **hundred ohms to a few kilohms** ✓ low, being a
forward-biased junction - which is why the preceding stage must be able to drive it.
**The three configurations compared.**
**common emitter**: high current, voltage and power gain; the general-purpose
amplifier ✓
**common base**: voltage gain but **no** current gain; used at high frequencies ✓
**common collector** (emitter follower): current gain but **no** voltage gain; used as
a **buffer**, matching a high-impedance source to a low-impedance load ✓
**Why the input cannot be across the collector.** That junction is **reverse biased** ✓
and would pass almost no signal current; its high resistance makes it suited to the
**output**, not the input.
**Reading the distractors.** **Emitter-collector** ✗ is the **output**.
**Collector-base** ✗ is the reverse-biased junction. **Anywhere** ✗ ignores the
configuration altogether ✓
∴ base – emitter.

Constructive interference needs a path difference of a **whole number of wavelengths**.
**Step 1 — state the condition.**
path difference = **nλ**, with n = 0, 1, 2, … ✓
**Step 2 — see why.** A path difference of one wavelength puts the two waves back
**in step** ✓ crest meeting crest and trough meeting trough, so the amplitudes add and
the intensity is a maximum.
**Step 3 — note the corresponding phase difference.**
Δφ = (2π/λ) x path difference = **2nπ** ✓
an exact whole number of cycles - which is the first option, and a correct statement
about the **phase**, not the **path**. Reading which quantity is asked for is the whole
difficulty.
**The destructive condition, for contrast.**
path difference = **(2n + 1)λ/2** ✓ an odd number of **half** wavelengths
phase difference = **(2n + 1)π** ✓
crest meets trough and they cancel - which is the third option here.
**The relation between the two measures.**
**Δφ = (2π/λ) x Δx** ✓
A path difference of λ corresponds to a phase difference of 2π; of λ/2, to π.
**Where the condition is applied.**
**Young's double slit**: d sin θ = nλ for a bright fringe ✓
**thin films**: 2µt = nλ or (n + ½)λ, depending on the phase change on reflection ✓
**diffraction gratings**: d sin θ = nλ, with n the order ✓
**Why interference needs coherence.** The two sources must maintain a **constant phase
relationship** ✓ Two independent lamps produce no visible fringes, because their
relative phase changes randomly every 10⁻⁸ s. Young's great insight was to derive both
beams from a **single** source.
**What happens to the energy.** It is **redistributed**, not created ✓ The bright
fringes gain exactly what the dark ones lose, and the average intensity across the
pattern equals the sum of the two beams.
**A worked instance.** Two sources 2 m and 2·0006 m from a point, with λ = 600 nm:
path difference = 0·6 mm = **1000λ** ✓ a whole number, so the point is **bright**.
**Reading the distractors.** **2nπ** ✗ is the **phase** condition. **(2n + 1)λ/2** ✗
and **(2n + 1)λ** ✗ are destructive and a mixture respectively ✓
∴ n λ.

Kinetic energy goes as the **square** of the momentum.
**Step 1 — write the relation.**
KE = **p²/(2m)** ✓
so for a given body, KE ∝ p².
**Step 2 — apply the 50% increase.**
p′ = 1·5p ✓
**Step 3 — find the new kinetic energy.**
KE′/KE = (1·5)²
= **2·25** ✓
**Step 4 — express as a percentage increase.**
increase = 2·25 − 1 = 1·25
= **125%** ✓
**Why the answer is 125 and not 225.** The energy becomes **2·25 times** its original
value, but the **increase** is 1·25 times - that is, 125% ✓ The 225% option is the
**new** energy as a percentage of the old, and it is the designed trap.
**A worked check.** Take p = 10 kg m s⁻¹ and m = 1 kg:
originally: KE = 100/2 = **50 J**
after: p = 15, KE = 225/2 = **112·5 J** ✓
increase = 62·5 J, which is **125%** of 50 J ✓
**Why the square appears.** Momentum is mv and energy is ½mv² ✓ so energy depends on
the **square** of the speed while momentum depends on it linearly. Eliminating v gives
KE = p²/2m.
**The corresponding change in speed.** Also **50%**, since p = mv and the mass is
fixed ✓ so the speed rises from v to 1·5v, and the energy from ½mv² to ½m(2·25v²).
**The general rule.** A fractional increase x in momentum gives a fractional increase
**(1 + x)² − 1 = 2x + x²** in energy ✓ For small x this is about **2x** - energy
changes roughly twice as fast as momentum.
**The companion question.** If instead the **energy** rose by 50%, the momentum would
rise by √1·5 − 1 = **22·5%** ✓ the relationship running the other way.
**Why this matters in practice.** It is why stopping distances grow so steeply with
speed ✓ and why a 50% faster vehicle carries 125% more kinetic energy to dissipate in
a crash.
**Reading the distractors.** **225%** ✗ is the new energy, not the increase. **25%** ✗
and **100%** ✗ correspond to momentum increases of 11·8% and 41·4% ✓
∴ 125%.

Surface gravity goes as **M/R²**, so halving both the mass and the radius **doubles**
it.
**Step 1 — write the relation.**
g = **GM/R²** ✓
**Step 2 — test each option.**
**both M and R doubled**: g′ = 2M/(2R)² = 2M/4R² = **g/2** ✗
**M halved, R the same**: g′ = **g/2** ✗
**both M and R halved**: g′ = (M/2)/(R/2)² = (M/2)/(R²/4) = **2g** ✓
**R halved, M the same**: g′ = M/(R/2)² = **4g** ✗
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Both the mass and the radius halved** gives twice the Earth's
gravity ✓
**Why halving both doubles g.** The mass contributes a factor of **½** and the radius a
factor of **4**, since it enters squared ✓ The net effect is 4 x ½ = **2**.
**What such a planet would be like.** Half the Earth's mass in half the radius means
**four times** the density ✓ about 22000 kg m⁻³ - denser than any known rock, and
denser even than osmium. It would be a very strange world, but the arithmetic is sound.
**Why the fourth option overshoots.** Keeping the mass while halving the radius gives
**4g**, not 2g ✓ The radius is the more powerful lever, because it is squared.
**A systematic way to see it.** Write g ∝ M R⁻² and scale M by a and R by b:
g′/g = **a/b²** ✓
option 1: 2/4 = 0·5; option 2: 0·5/1 = 0·5; option 3: **0·5/0·25 = 2** ✓; option 4:
1/0·25 = 4. One formula settles all four.
**Real planetary values, for scale.**
Mars: M = 0·107, R = 0·532, so g = 0·107/0·283 = **0·38** of Earth's ✓
Jupiter: M = 318, R = 11·2, so g = 318/125 = **2·5** ✓ - a real planet with gravity
close to the one described.
**Why Jupiter is not an exact match.** It is **more** massive and **larger**, not less
and smaller ✓ The same ratio can be reached by many combinations, which is the point of
the question.
**What would also double.** The **escape velocity** v_e = √(2GM/R) scales as
√(a/b) = √(0·5/0·5) = **1** ✓ so it would be **unchanged** - a nice illustration that
different quantities scale differently.
∴ Both the mass and radius of the planet are half as that of Earth.

The most elastic substance is the one with the **largest Young's modulus** - **steel**.
**Step 1 — define elasticity properly.** In physics, elasticity measures a body's
**resistance** to deformation and its ability to **recover** its shape ✓ The measure is
**Young's modulus**:
Y = stress/strain ✓
A **large** Y means a **highly elastic** material.
**Step 2 — compare the four.**
**steel**: Y ≈ **2 x 10¹¹ Pa** ✓ the largest by far
**copper**: Y ≈ 1·1 x 10¹¹ Pa
**rubber**: Y ≈ **10⁶ Pa** - a hundred thousand times smaller ✓
**sponge**: smaller still, and largely plastic rather than elastic
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Steel** has the highest elasticity ✓
**Why this seems backwards at first.** In everyday speech "elastic" means **easily
stretched**, which describes rubber ✓ In physics it means the opposite: a material
that **resists** deformation and springs back exactly. Steel deforms very little under
a large stress and returns precisely to its original length - the ideal elastic
behaviour.
**The numbers that settle it.** A 1 m steel wire of 1 mm² cross-section under 100 N
stretches by
ΔL = FL/(AY) = 100/(10⁻⁶ x 2 x 10¹¹) = **0·5 mm** ✓
The same wire in rubber would stretch by **100 m** - if it did not break first.
**Why rubber is not truly elastic.** Its stress-strain curve is strongly **non-linear**
and shows **hysteresis** ✓ It does not obey Hooke's law, and energy is lost on each
cycle - which is why a bouncing rubber ball warms up and why tyres heat on the road.
**Why steel is used for springs and cables.** High Y means a predictable, linear,
fully recoverable response ✓ A steel spring obeys Hooke's law accurately over a wide
range, which is what a spring must do.
**The three elastic moduli.**
**Young's** Y: stretching ✓
**bulk** K: uniform compression ✓
**rigidity** G: shearing ✓
Steel leads on all three.
**Where rubber wins instead.** In the **range** of strain it can take ✓ Steel yields at
about 0·2% strain; rubber stretches to several hundred per cent. Large deformation and
high elasticity are quite different virtues.
∴ Steel.

Two forces act: **gravity**, always straight down, and **air resistance**, always
**opposite to the velocity**.
**Step 1 — identify the forces.** Once the ball has left the hand, only two forces act:
**weight mg**, vertically **downward**, constant throughout ✓
**air drag**, directed **opposite to the instantaneous velocity** ✓
**Step 2 — find the velocity at X.** X is early in the flight, on the **rising** part
of the trajectory, so the ball is moving **upward and to the right** ✓
**Step 3 — find the drag direction.** Opposite to that - **downward and to the
left** ✓
**Step 4 — assemble the diagram.** One arrow pointing **straight down** (weight) and
one pointing **down-left** at an angle (drag) ✓ That is the first figure.
**Why the drag must oppose the velocity exactly.** Air resistance arises from the
relative motion of the ball through the air ✓ It is always **antiparallel** to the
velocity, whatever direction the ball happens to be travelling.
**How the picture changes along the trajectory.**
**rising**, moving up-right: drag points **down-left** ✓
at the **top**, moving horizontally right: drag points **horizontally left**, and the
only vertical force is gravity ✓
**falling**, moving down-right: drag points **up-left** ✓
The weight never changes; the drag swings right round.
**What the drag does to the trajectory.** It makes the path **asymmetric** ✓ The
descending half is steeper and shorter than the ascending half, and the range is less
than the vacuum value. A real cricket ball's path is noticeably lopsided.
**Why there is no forward force.** Nothing pushes the ball along once it has left the
hand ✓ The commonest misconception in projectile problems is an imagined "force of
motion" in the direction of travel. Newton's first law forbids it.
**The magnitude of the drag.** Roughly **½C_DρAv²** ✓ so it grows with the **square**
of the speed - strongest at launch, weakest at the top of the flight where the ball is
slowest.
**Why the ball is not in free fall.** With drag present the acceleration is **not** g,
and it is not even constant in direction ✓ The simple projectile formulas no longer
apply, which is what makes real ballistics hard.
**Reading the distractors.** Any figure with an arrow pointing **forward** ✗ invents a
driving force. Any with the drag pointing **down-right** ✗ has it along the velocity
rather than against it ✓
∴ the first figure.
